senses.sense_definition: Of, relating to, or resembling a lion; lionlike.

examples.text: The elderly author was famous for his thick mane of hair and distinctly <w>leonine</w> appearance.
With a broad chest and a heavy stride, he moved across the room with <w>leonine</w> confidence.

senses.sense_definition: Displaying facial features that resemble a lion as a consequence of disease, particularly advanced leprosy.

examples.text: The physician immediately noted the patient's <w>leonine</w> facies during the clinical examination.
Extensive tissue infiltration caused by the infection produced a marked <w>leonine</w> expression.

senses.sense_definition: Of or relating to any of the popes named Leo, especially Pope Leo IV or Pope Leo XIII.

examples.text: Tourists walked along the fortified ancient walls of the <w>leonine</w> quarter surrounding the Vatican.
The historical document outlined the administrative reforms enacted during the <w>leonine</w> papacy.

senses.sense_definition: Relating to a style of Latin verse characterised by internal rhyme, usually between the middle and the end of the line.

examples.text: Medieval monks composed intricate hymns using <w>leonine</w> rhyme to aid memorisation.
The manuscript contains several <w>leonine</w> verses celebrating the founding of the abbey.

senses.sense_definition: Alternative letter-case form of <w>leonine</w>, relating to popes named Leo or to verse with internal rhyme.

examples.text: Scholars continue to study the rhythmic patterns found in traditional <w>Leonine</w> meter.
The defensive barrier protecting the Vatican was originally part of the <w>Leonine</w> wall.

senses.sense_definition: A medieval verse, especially in Latin hexameter or pentameter, featuring an internal rhyme between the middle and end of each line.

examples.text: The scholar translated several medieval <w>leonines</w> that had been recorded in the margins.
He delighted in composing modern <w>leonines</w> that imitated the style of early monastic poetry.

senses.sense_definition: A thirteenth-century debased European coin circulated in England as an imitation penny until banned by Edward I.

examples.text: Merchants routinely tested silver currency to identify any fraudulent <w>leonines</w> imported from the continent.
Royal decrees forbade the circulation of debased coins, explicitly naming <w>leonines</w> alongside pollards and crocards.

senses.sense_definition: Alternative letter-case form of <w>leonine</w>, denoting the debased medieval coin.

examples.text: The royal proclamation strictly ordered that foreign <w>Leonines</w> be removed from legal circulation.
He paid the fine using an assortment of outdated silver pieces and debased <w>Leonines</w>.
